asks: How is a report matched to a fact, and a process to a run?
answer: A report is matched to a fact by exact keys, never by nearness in time alone. A file report matches a file fact when the computer and the path are the same and the report falls between the two checkpoints the fact covers. Where a report falls is read from its source's own numbers, not from a clock: at each checkpoint the probe is told of it and writes a line that marks it in its count, so a report numbered before the mark falls before the checkpoint even when it arrives after. A report that no mark places is not compared, and stays unverified. A connection report matches a connection fact when the computer, the local port, the host and the port are the same and the times overlap. A process belongs to a run when a walk up its parents, or its group where the system has one, reaches the launch of an agent program; when the two reach different launches, it belongs to no run, and both runs are named. A fact with no report stays unattributed. A report that the facts contradict gets a mismatch, and a report with nothing to compare it with stays simply unverified. A process whose chain is broken, by a gap or a missing parent, belongs to no run, and what it wrote is unattributed. When several runs report writing the same path between the same two checkpoints, the change is not shared out: it is unattributed, and the runs that reported it are named. Tests with reports made up by a hostile program check each case. To find out: how the mark is placed, and how a write the computer had not yet saved to its disk at the checkpoint is placed.
